southIndianStatus.productLedExplanation: Kozhukattai is a Tamil Nadu and Kerala festival dumpling with no pan-Indian equivalent. The name is Tamil, the preparation is South Indian, and the ritual context (Ganesh Chaturthi, Karthigai) is specifically South Indian.
southIndianStatus.flavorLedExplanation: Filled with coconut-jaggery or sesame-jaggery, the flavor profile is distinctly South Indian — no northern sweet uses this combination in this steamed dumpling form.
southIndianStatus.overallSummary: Kozhukattai is South India's answer to modak — but it predates the comparison and belongs to Tamil Nadu's festival calendar in its own right.

stateSpeciality.origin: Kozhukattai is a Sangam-era preparation — steamed rice dumplings filled with coconut, jaggery, and sesame. The shape varies by region: pointed oval for Ganesh, round for prasadam. The name itself is Tamil.
stateSpeciality.culturalSignificance: The primary offering for Ganesh Chaturthi in Tamil Nadu and Kerala. Also made for Karthigai Deepam and Varalakshmi Vratam. Considered the most auspicious sweet to offer to Pillayar (Ganesh).
stateSpeciality.storytelling: The trick to good kozhukattai is the thickness of the rice flour shell — thin enough to steam through in twelve minutes, thick enough not to crack when lifted. The filling — fresh coconut mixed with jaggery that has been cooked to just before crystallization — must be cool before stuffing. Every grandmother in Tamil Nadu has a preferred shape, a preferred filling ratio, and a strong opinion about anyone who gets either wrong.
stateSpeciality.bestSeason: Ganesh Chaturthi (August-September) is the primary season. Also Karthigai Deepam (November-December).

functionalCallouts.explanation: Kozhukattai is steamed, not fried — making it the lowest-fat festival sweet in the South Indian calendar. The only fat comes from natural coconut in the filling.
The outer shell is made entirely from rice flour — naturally gluten-free. A festival sweet that those with wheat sensitivities can consume without modification.

productDescriptors.title: Shaped Before Dawn
productDescriptors.descriptor: Good kozhukattai is shaped before the family wakes up. The rice flour dough has to be the right temperature — warm but not sticky. The filling has to be the right consistency — cool and firm, not wet. Each dumpling is pressed into its shape by hand, sealed carefully, and arranged in the steamer in the right order. A batch of sixty takes two hours. They are eaten in twelve minutes.
productDescriptors.rationale: The '60 made in 2 hours, eaten in 12 minutes' contrast communicates craft without complaint — it makes the consumer feel the value of what they are about to eat.

productDescriptors.title: Ganesh's Sweet, Not Ours
productDescriptors.descriptor: Kozhukattai is not a snack. It is an offering. In Tamil Nadu, Pillayar Chaturthi begins with this — steam rising from the steel plate, the specific smell of coconut and jaggery heating together, and the understanding that you make this for Ganesh before you make it for yourself. What remains after the offering is the best sweet you will have all year.
productDescriptors.rationale: Positioning kozhukattai as 'Ganesh's sweet first, yours second' is psycho-logically powerful — it adds spiritual permission and exclusivity to the product without any false claims.

productDescriptors.title: Twelve Minutes in the Steamer. No Shortcuts.
productDescriptors.descriptor: The shell has to be thin enough to cook through in twelve minutes. Too thick and the inside stays raw; too thin and it cracks when you lift it. The jaggery in the filling has to be cooled before going in, or the shell softens in the wrong way. There is a reason kozhukattai is made at home less often now — and that is exactly why each one in this box matters.
productDescriptors.rationale: Acknowledging that 'kozhukattai is made at home less often now' frames the purchase as preserving something being lost — stronger than any positive claim.
